transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I’m Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, hello, Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I'm Tom. I, uh... well, my daughter actually insisted I come in, but I suppose she's right. It's just... it's a very difficult thing to talk about, especially at my age. You know, you get to be 78, you think you've got yourself figured out, you think you've seen it all and handled it all. I worked hard my whole life, raised a family, retired... I should be enjoying my quiet time, maybe doing some woodworking in the garage, watching the birds, that sort of thing. But instead, I'm... I'm dealing with this terrible problem with food. 

It's not just eating too much at Thanksgiving, you know? It's... what scares me most is that once I start eating, it feels like I completely lose the reins. It's like my hands just keep reaching for more, opening cupboards, unwrapping things, even while my own brain is screaming at me, telling myself, "Tom, stop this right now. You don't need this, you're going to feel terrible." But it's like I'm a passenger in my own body. I just can't stop it once it starts. It's exhausting, Doctor, truly exhausting, and frankly, it's humiliating to feel so out of control of my own two hands.
Can you tell me more about these episodes where you feel like you lose control over your eating? How often do they happen, and what kinds of foods are you typically eating during these times?

Well, it's... it's usually in the afternoons. My wife, Mary, she volunteers at the church on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and my daughter is at work, so the house is just... it's very quiet. Too quiet, sometimes. I sit in my recliner, trying to watch the news or maybe a history program, but my mind just wanders. And before I know it, I'm in the kitchen. 

I'll start with something small, maybe just a slice of bread. But then... then it just escalates. I don't even know how to explain it properly, Doctor. It's like a frenzy. I'll go through the rest of that loaf of bread, just plain or maybe I'll slather half a jar of peanut butter on it. Then I'll find a package of cookies—those little chocolate chip ones my granddaughter likes when she visits—and I'll eat the whole sleeve. Then I'm opening the fridge, pulling out whatever leftovers are in there... meatloaf, cold pasta, it doesn't even matter if they go together or if they're even heated up. I just eat them. And then, to top it all off, I'll dig into a carton of ice cream. I can eat half a gallon of butter pecan just standing there at the counter. 

All of this, Doctor, all of this food... I can eat it all in one sitting, just shoveling it in, before I even really look up and realize what I've done. It's like I'm in a trance. And it's happening a lot. I'd say... gosh, it's got to be at least four or five times a week now. Sometimes more if it's a particularly long day. I just... I never thought I'd be a man who couldn't control himself around a loaf of bread, you know? It's just shameful. I look at the empty wrappers and the dirty plates and I just think, 'Tom, what on earth is wrong with you?' It's a terrible, terrible feeling.
After these episodes of overeating, do you ever make yourself vomit, use laxatives, or try to exercise excessively to make up for what you've eaten?

Well, Doctor... yes. Yes, I do. It's... it's the part I hate the most, if I'm being honest. After I've eaten all that food—the bread, the cookies, the ice cream, just all of it sitting there heavy in my stomach—the panic sets in. It's a terrible panic, like I'm going to burst, or like all that food is just going to turn into pure fat right then and there. My heart starts racing, and I just feel so sick with myself. 

So, I... I go to the bathroom. I make sure the door is locked, even if Mary isn't home, just out of habit, I suppose. And I... I make myself bring it all back up. It's awful, truly awful. I'm a grown man, 78 years old, leaning over the toilet like a sick child. It hurts my throat, it makes my eyes water, and sometimes my chest aches afterward. But in the moment, it feels like the only way to undo the damage I've just done. Like I can just erase it, you know? 

And... and that's not all. Sometimes, if I can't bring it up, or if I just feel like there's still too much left inside me, I'll take laxatives. I started buying them a few months ago. I go to a different pharmacy across town so the pharmacist at my usual place doesn't ask questions. I'll take them because I'm just so terrified that all that food is going to stay in me, that it's going to stick to my ribs and I'll just keep expanding. I know it's not right, Doctor. I know taking pills like that isn't how they're meant to be used, but the fear of the food staying inside me is just overwhelming. It's a vicious cycle, it really is. I eat until I can't breathe, and then I do whatever I can to get rid of it. I'm just so tired of living like this.

Tom, when you're not in the middle of one of these eating episodes, do you still feel like you're losing control over other parts of your life, or is that sense of losing control limited only to when you're eating?

No, no, that's the strangest part of all this, Doctor. If you look at the rest of my life... well, I've always been a very disciplined man. You ask Mary, she'll tell you. I keep a very tight ship. My garage, for instance—every tool has its place, outlined on the pegboard. I handle all our finances, balance the checkbook down to the penny every Sunday evening right after dinner, just like I've done for the last fifty years. I've always been the one people rely on to keep things steady. 

Even back when I was working, before I retired, I was a floor supervisor at the plant for twenty years because I knew how to keep things running smoothly, no surprises, no nonsense. So, no, I don't feel out of control anywhere else in my life. Not at all. I wake up at 6 AM sharp, I read the paper, I maintain the yard... I mean, just last week I completely reorganized the attic because I couldn't stand the holiday boxes being out of order from when my son brought them down last Christmas. I like order. I need order. 

It's just... it's just the food. And I think that's why it's so incredibly maddening! I can control a crew of fifty men on a factory floor, I can manage a fixed retirement budget in this crazy economy, I can keep every blade of grass in my lawn exactly two inches high, but you put me alone in my own kitchen on a Tuesday afternoon and suddenly I'm a completely different person. It makes absolutely no sense to me. Outside of those episodes, I'm just regular old Tom, steady as a rock. It's only when I start eating that the wheels completely fall off the wagon.

Tom, have these episodes of overeating and the way you deal with them afterward affected your ability to participate in social activities, spend time with family, or take care of daily responsibilities?

Well, yes. Yes, it has, and that's the part that really breaks my heart, Doctor. It really does. You see, for the last five years, ever since I really settled into my retirement routine, I was part of this local garden group. We’d meet up at the community plots over on Elm Street. I was in charge of the heirloom tomatoes—Big Boys, Early Girls, Cherokee Purples, you name it, I grew them. We'd get together on Wednesday mornings, have a thermos of coffee, talk about soil pH and fertilizer... it was a good group of fellows. But... well, I haven't been in months. I just stopped going. I told them my arthritis was acting up, but that was a lie. 

The truth is, Wednesday mornings became this window where I knew Mary would be out at the grocery store, and all I could think about was... well, the food. I’d be sitting there on Tuesday night, already planning my whole Wednesday morning around what I could eat and how I could get rid of it before she got back with the groceries. And if I went to the garden group, I’d miss that window. I chose the food over my friends. 

And it's not just the garden group, Doctor. It's my own family. We've always done Sunday dinners. For decades, it's been a tradition. My daughter brings my granddaughter over, Mary cooks a roast or maybe a nice baked ham... but lately, I just can't sit through it. I’ve been pulling away from those meals, too. I make up excuses. I say my stomach is upset, or I eat just a few bites and go sit in the other room while they finish. Because if I sit there with all that food in front of me, I’m terrified I’ll lose control right there at the table and just start shoveling it in. Or worse, I’ll eat a normal plate, but then that terrible panic sets in, and I’ll have to excuse myself to the bathroom while they're all sitting right there in the living room. 

I'm just so terribly worried someone will notice what I'm doing. What if Mary hears me getting sick? What if my granddaughter wants to use the bathroom and the door is locked? The shame of it afterward, Doctor, it's just heavy. It's like a physical weight I carry around all day. I'm constantly worried someone is going to look at me and just *know* what a mess I am. So I just isolate myself. I stay in my recliner. I pull away from the people I love because hiding this secret... it takes up all my energy. I never thought I'd be a man who skips out on his own family just to sneak food in his own kitchen, but that's exactly what it's come to. It's just completely taken over my schedule, my mind... everything.
